"Sell it! Sell it!": Recent Translations of Lunyu David Schaberg University of California, Los Angeles Works reviewed, in order of discussion: Roger T. Ames and Henry Rosemont, Jr. The Analects of Confucius: A Philosophical Translation. New York: Ballantine Books, 1998. D.C. Lau. Confucius: The Analects (Lun yii). Second ed., Hong Kong: Chinese University Press, 1992. Raymond Dawson. Confucius: The Analects. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1993. Simon Leys. The Analects of Confucius. New York: W.W. Norton & Company, 1997. Chichung Huang. The Analects of Confucius (Lun Yu). Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997. David Hinton. The Analects: Confucius. Washington, D.C.: Counterpoint, 1998. E. Bruce Brooks and A. Taeko Brooks. The Original Analects: Sayings of Confucius and His Successors. New York: Columbia University Press, 1998. Behind the survival of any ancient text into the present century lies an initial investment of some sort, small or large, some commitment of resources to support the transmission of old words to new readers. At the very least, even where climate aids the conservation effort-as in Egypt or Central Asia-someone had to have acquired the tools and training to write, and had to have had something worth writing. Elsewhere, greater investments, whether in more durable media or in the construction of shelters where texts might be hidden away from damp and thieves, did promote survival, even if they could not ensure it; witness the unmatched importance of tomb and trove finds in the study of early Chinese writing. Above-ground manuscript transmission is costlier still: for any pre-Qin text to have reached us by this means, it must have been recopied at least enough times to outrun the decay of exposed bamboo, silk, or paper, and it must have been disseminated widely enough in every generation, and with enough prestige, to justify that recopying. Of all these requirements, perhaps the costliest is prestige, which implies a commitment from wealthy individuals or groups. However it is achieved, cultural memory is expensive. In the world of texts as in the world of finance, the densest concentrations of capital do not dissipate overnight. They change hands and are converted in various ways, but their fame tends to encourage people to fight for them against entropy. If the end of an examination system or the coming of a revolutionary campaign changes the value of a text, it rarely bankrupts it, since investors are numerous and confident ? 116 Chinese Literature: Essays, Articles, Reviews 23 (2001) enough to ride out the threat. Contact with foreign cultures may flood the market with new writings, but it also inevitably brings in new investors for an important indigenous text, outsiders who recognize value and want a part of it. From this perspective, the prominence of a work like the Lunyu, and the continual publication of new annotations and translations in China and abroad, have little to do with the expression of a putative essence of the Chinese national character, and much to do with perceived opportunities to convert the text's value into new forms. Like other traveling texts-the Hebrew Bible comes to mind-the Lunyu has outlived many social, intellectual, and ethnic homelands, and owes its very existence to its adaptability. The publication by major houses of six new English translations of the Lunyu in the last decade, with the reissuing of an older one in a revised, bilingual version, attests to the presence of a very strong profit motive. Neither this observation nor the phenomenon itself is crass. Translations can and should be measured according to standards of accuracy, accessibility, and elegance. However, these criteria hardly account for all of the factors that influence a complicated cultural exchange like the ongoing reception of Confucianism in the English-speaking world. Every one of the translations under review, from the least accurate to the most painstaking, appeals to a particular reading public and (if online retailers' sales figures are accurate) is reaching that public in a way that should please the publishers. With one or two exceptions, the process of intellectual product diversification that has brought the Lunyu to these niche readerships has not entailed any betrayal of the prevailing standards of translation. The question is not so much whether any of the works is good, or how good it is, but what and whom it is good for. And all of them are good for extending the Lunyu's appeal to readers who otherwise might not have considered the text important. The translation of Ames and Rosemont will give encouragement to readers seeking a pragmatist alternative to dire warnings about a clash of civilizations. D.C. Lau's 1992 version differs from his 1979 Penguin version (still in print) in many details of phrasing, but in few basic matters of interpretation, and will continue to attract many with its well-rounded, sententious renditions of the aphorisms. Both of these translations include the Chinese text, and will be handy for readers who (like many of my Los Angeles undergraduates) come to the Lunyu with some knowledge of the language. Dawson's volume is slim, literal, affordable, and accompanied by scant but respectable explanatory material. Leys' is freer, tarter, and more readable as a model of English aphoristic style than any other. Huang's takes care to note the alternate interpretations of many passages that any serious student of the Lunyu must know, even if he or she is reading the work in translation. Hinton's, at a price, makes the Lunyu more colloquial than any other version, and may reach the burgeoning New Age readership more effectively than any other. Brooks and Brooks quite explicitly aim to engage both sinologists and non-specialist readers who are interested in the problem of precise dating of early texts. To stop with a round of praise-diverse jobs, but jobs well done!-would hardly suffice. Even taking into account the exigencies of niche marketing, all of the translations presume a shared fundamental promise, that is, to turn over to us something of value All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

SCHABERG Recent Translations of Lunyu 117 derived ultimately from Confucius and his earliest followers. They claim to deliver the goods. Yet all of them fall short in one way or another. In the more modest efforts, the failings are minor but unnecessary: principles adduced to justify the publication of a new version are carelessly subverted in the course of the translation. Predictably or not, the two most ambitious efforts-discussed in the first and last sections of this review-have produced the most remarkable failures, and differ from the others in that these failures derive from the stated motives of the projects. One might, in my view, choose the translation by Lau, Dawson, Leys, or Huang, depending on the circumstances, and present it to an interested friend or to a group of undergraduates (surely the largest market) with few qualms and few warnings. Not so with the studies by Ames and Rosemont and Brooks and Brooks, which without a good deal of qualification and critical preparation will only lead new audiences seriously astray. Confucianism as a Language without History The "philosophical" translation of the Lunyu by Roger Ames and Henry Rosemont, Jr. is billed on the cover as "a new translation based on the Dingzhou fragments and other recent archaeological finds." Like other translations in Ballantine's useful "Classics of Ancient China" series, including Ames's excellent version of the Sunzi, it does reflect research in archaeologically recovered texts, and helpfully includes the Chinese original for the main text under translation. The philosophical project, carried out in a long introduction and in one of the two appendices (the first being devoted to an account of the Dingzhou finds), is linked to a hypothesis about written Chinese: We believe that readers of this translation of the Analects will give it credence in proportion to the credence they give to our account of language, speech, and writing in general, the Chinese written language in particular, and to the cosmology we have described for all who employed this written language. (p. 285) The cosmology in question is the one proposed in such well-known publications as Thinking Through Confucius, by Ames and David Hall; as it has been subjected to critique elsewhere, I will not address it except in passing.' The account of language, which has its clearest antecedents in earlier work by Rosemont, appears to have reached its fullest development in the course of this collaboration. It involves an extraordinary assertion about what the authors refer to as "the basically nonverbal nature of literary Chinese" (p. 294): Our own thesis is that the classical Chinese language-the language in which the books of the Analects were composed-is unique, being sharply distinct not only 1See, among other collaborative works, David L. Hall and Roger T. Ames, Thinking Through Confucius (Albany: State University of New York Press, 1987). For a recent critique relating to views of language, see Robert Wardy, Aristotle in China: Language, Categories, and Translation (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2000), pp. 30-34. 118 Chinese Literature: Essays, Articles, Reviews 23 (2001) from all non-sinitic languages, but from spoken Chinese as well, both ancient and modern. (p. 36) The reader of classical Chinese knows well that there is a subtlety and a richness to the characters and their arrangements that allow a communicative style that can be as effective as it is terse, and unattainable verbally. . . In classical Chinese this extraordinary kind of communication is made possible semantically by the fact that each lexical item carries all of its meanings with it on every occasion of its use, and the concatenation of two or more characters therefore associates all of the meanings of each one with the others. It is unlikely that many associations would be lost in reading, because even though word order was important, it was not firmly fixed in the literary language, so the reader would have to examine almost every passage several times, attending to multiple possible orderings of the characters before settling on an interpretation. This type of communication was further enhanced by the pictorial, imagistic, and aesthetic quality of the characters. One way to relate two or more characters in a passage would be to see that they all contained a certain element; the characters for "virtue (de f)" and "thought (si J,)," for example, could be associated together at least visually because they both contain the character for "heart-and-mind (xin 4,)." The majority of the basic 2500+ characters which formed the lexicon of classical Chinese are constituted in the same graphic way; hence, what might be overlooked completely or passed off lightly as mere punning or ungrammatical in an alphabetic language could be employed seriously for expressive and communicative purposes in an ideographic one. (pp. 42-43) In short, Ames and Rosemont argue that the written Chinese of the Lunyu is an artificial language that conveys meaning not only through means borrowed from speech, but also through visual means, i.e. through the significant juxtaposition of pictographs, ideographs, and/or portions of same. On this hypothesis they stake the credibility of their translation. Even if Ames and Rosemont made an effort in the course of their translation to show how the visual hypothesis might help solve problems of interpretation-and they do not-the hypothesis would be untenable, at least as presently expressed. It rests upon premises that few linguists or philologists could endorse, and ignores much in the way of contradictory evidence, including evidence from the Dingzhou manuscripts themselves. The vision of Confucian thought that it in turn is called upon to support may or may not be creditable, either as philosophy or as a quasi-religious declaration of faith in reinterpreted scripture. But one fundamental aspect of this vision-the claim that it is rooted in historical and linguistic realities-is poorly defended, and will serve mainly to perpetuate among Ballantine's non-specialist readers a familiar but flawed vision of Chinese uniqueness. The problems begin with a radically dehistoricized view of written and spoken Chinese. For all that readers of the introduction and appendices might gather, no distinction is to be drawn between "classical" and "literary" Chinese, terms that the authors use interchangeably. This language, whatever it is called, stretches unbroken and barely altered, from oracle bone inscriptions to certain contemporary genres of All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

SCHABERG Recent Translations of Lunyu 119 formal writing. It is set apart from the spoken language (also largely dehistoricized, its grammatical and phonological changes ignored) by its supposed reliance upon pictographic and ideographic techniques that prevailed in its earliest stages. In its very origins, Ames and Rosemont argue, the writing system bypassed the spoken word by being "representations of objects and ideas" rather than of sounds (p. 290). As the "highly abbreviated linguistic forms" of the oracle bones became "models for all written composition over a period of time" (p. 292), origins became destiny: The written patterns found in the Shang materials continued to be exemplified in the classical literature throughout the period of its paramountcy, a time span of thirty-five centuries. The assumption that there is a direct line betweeen the linguistic patterns found on the oracle bones and the classical literature that emerged from these beginnings is generally correct. (p. 292) One could hardly fault the reader who comes away with the impression that, apart from trivial differences in the form of characters, little distinguishes the language of a divinatory scapula from that of a Western Zhou bronze inscription, a Lunyu aphorism, a Han Yu essay, or Sanguozhi yanyi •_ ,, . The "direct line" referred to in the passage cited above is a mirage, and one that comes into view only because of a refusal to define the "linguistic patterns" referred to further on in the passage. Ames and Rosemont assume, as if it were a given, that the relevant patterns are those characterizing the construction and syntactical arrangement of graphs as a visual system of signification. But even if this assumption were safe, their visual hypothesis would be questionable at best, and only for a brief period in the early history of writing; for the whole thirty-five century stretch it would simply be wrong. Consider the logic of the following passage: David Keightley, reflecting on the insurmoutable [sic] problem of pronunciation of Shang graphs, has observed: Since there is no evidence of rhyme in the oracle inscriptions, the traditional and even modern approach to their study has been resolutely graphemic.2 Consequently, we have morphological as well as phonetic support for considering the early written forms to have their own communicative function without having been transcribed speech; at this stage, much information was communicated visually. (p. 290) On the contrary: Keightley's observation had only to do with the nature of scholarship about the inscriptions, not with the nature of the written language itself, and in no way supports the conclusions here drawn from it. Observed patterns in the historical development of the Chinese writing system-patterns almost entirely disregarded by 2The authors cite David N. Keightley, Sources of Shang History: The Oracle-Bone Inscriptions of Bronze Age China (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1978), p. 67. All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

120 Chinese Literature: Essays, Articles, Reviews 23 (2001) Ames and Rosemont-strongly suggest that a purely visual communication of information, if it ever existed, was almost immediately overwhelmed by the recycling of characters as rebuses, that is, for purposes that rendered the original visual referent wholly irrelevant.3 Without suggesting that early Chinese inscriptions and texts are merely direct transcriptions of speech-a view that the authors rightly reject (pp. 41-42, 304-05)-one must recognize that something other than visuality was playing a role in the development of the written language. Features of the written language as it is known from the centuries just before and after the life of Confucius further undermine the visual hypothesis. Ames and Rosemont argue that an abundance of visual information in a written passage compensates for a poverty of phonetic information; phonemes being few and homonyms many, they say, written Chinese is often ambiguous when read aloud, though intelligible when seen (p. 297). But the survival of rhymed texts, including but not limited to the Shi •, has made possible approximate phonetic reconstructions of the readings of graphs, and has shown a greater wealth of phonemes than Ames and Rosemont seem willing to acknowledge.4 And in any case, even if it were true that written passages often yielded oral/ aural ambiguities, that would not in itself prove the existence of a special language, or the dominance of visual semantics over ordinary modes of reference in written language.5 Further, several features of the early writing system revealed by 3See William G. Boltz, "Language and Writing," in The Cambridge History of Ancient China: From the Origins of Civilization to 221 B.C., edited by Michael Loewe and Edward L. Shaughnessy (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999), p. 110. 4A passage on p. 297 is particularly alarming, and typical in its unjustified denial of historical change: There exist now only about 420 different syllables in modern Mandarin. Thus the inventive scribe seeking a character to represent a new vocabulary item might have had from three to a hundred different forms to pick from, all of which were pronounced almost exactly the same. On what basis would the scribe pick one over another? Surely it would be a semantically motivated choice. For instance, if he wanted to represent in written form the sound / wu / which meant "to lie and deceive," "to slander," he would obviously use the pictogram denoting speech (yan -) as the radical element of compound character. And among the many lexical items pronounced /wu /, the scribe might have a range of homophones from which to choose. "To not have I," "martial :," "do not fI," and "sorcerer T," for example, would all be pronounced the same. He might rather creatively pick the character wu which approximates "sorcerer" in meaning to be the phonetic element, especially if he remembered that sorcerers were usually considered to be suspicious folk in ancient China and were not to be trusted. Thus the character wu meaning "to lie and deceive" would be represented in written form as "the words of a sorcerer"-yet be classified among the phonograms and not the ideograms. If one is not shocked by the bizarre (accidental?) suggestion that a modern Mandarin- speaking scribe could freely invent new characters, or by the citation of Mandarin readings in an argument that quite clearly calls for reconstructed Old Chinese readings, then one must at least be disappointed to learn that the graphs cited very possibly all had different readings in Old Chinese; while Karlgren gives them the same reconstruction in Grammata Serica Recensa, they are different in the system of Sergei Starostin, which can be consulted at <http://starling.rinet.ru/intrtext.htm>. The examples cited may handily disprove the case they are meant to prove. 5Ames and Rosemont argue that the price paid for brevity in written forms is ambiguity: their example is the sports-page headline "Salmon Biting Off Puget Coast" (p. 297). SCHABERG Recent Translations of Lunyu 121 archaeologically recovered texts-ways of handling word families, historical changes in the phonetic components chosen for the representation of certain words, and extraordinary liberties taken by individual scribes, who occasionally wrote the same word with two or even three different graphs in the same manuscript-all challenge the authors' vision of a written language isolated from speech; and all go unacknowledged by the authors. If the hypothesis were built upon an accurate view of the history of Chinese graphs, it would nevertheless have to take grammar into account. After all, the utterances that Ames and Rosemont are interested in are not monosyllables, as their focus on graphs might suggest, but strings of words; and grammar is the art of stringing words together meaningfully. One of the most surprising features of the defense of the hypothesis is that it does not-despite a brief discussion of "The Classical Chinese Language: Syntactical Considerations" (pp. 300-05)-address the glaring historical fact of grammatical change. It is only by lumping together all Chinese writing (with the exception of some relatively late vernacular texts) as "classical" / "literary" Chinese that the authors can make a case for the survival of an early visual language into later periods. Such a language, if it had existed, would presumably have been resistant or even impervious to grammatical change, since (as the authors claim in their account of syntax) it would simply repeat patterns found in memorized texts, presumably patterns tested out first on the Shang oracle bones. But anyone who has struggled to translate a Shang or Western Zhou inscription, or anyone (including Ames and Rosemont) who has read the archaic language found, e.g., in Lunyu 2.21 and 20.1, knows very well that written Chinese registered a great deal of grammatical change in the first millennium of its existence, and that this change was in no way dependent upon the strengths or weaknesses of the writing system. Readers who have compared Lunyu with Shiji E, or who have noticed that late and spurious guwen chapters of the Shu a play at early Zhou grammar and get it wrong, can make little sense of a theory of written Chinese that ignores grammatical change. Written Chinese became a literary language when and to the extent that its grammar ceased to change, having fallen out of contact with spoken forms of the language. This moment of petrification is generally thought to have arrived sometime during the Han. It is rarely pushed back before the Han, and perhaps never-before now-to the Shang. In one typical periodization, the grammar of the oracle bones differs significantly from that of Western Zhou texts (bronze inscriptions and parts of Shi, Shu, and Yi i;), while the Lunyu and certain other Warring States texts represent yet a third stage, a properly "classical" period that provided models for later prose.6 Readers of Yang Xiong's l (53 B.C.-A.D. 18) Fayan (-, a text written in direct imitation of the language and style of the Lunyu, might favor an even finer periodization, one that Eagleton, citing two equally amusing examples, rightly observes that "there is no kind of writing which cannot, given sufficient ingenuity, be read as estranging"; but no one is led astray by ambiguous headlines or public notices, since a social context guides interpretation. See Eagleton, Literary Theory: An Introduction (Oxford: Basil Blackwell, 1983), pp. 6-7. 6Boltz, "Language and Writing," pp. 88-91. All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

122 Chinese Literature: Essays, Articles, Reviews 23 (2001) reflects the differences between the archaizing Fayan and more standard Han texts. However you cut it, much of the Lunyu was written down before the coming of standard classical, with its relatively simple, fixed grammatical patterns; and it was written down well after a (perhaps imaginary) purely pictographic stage of the written language. If the written language of the Lunyu had any principles of order at all, beyond the mere wadding-together of brush-painted ideas, then these principles could have derived only from the grammar of speech. If it be argued that visual communication of meaning is secondary and supplementary to the representation of the spoken word and its grammar (a weaker form of the hypothesis, and one that Ames and Rosemont do not adopt), then one must ask again how the scribes of the Warring States could have taken such liberties in their writing-in which graphs are often chosen purely for their phonetic value-and how even a first century B.C. text like the Dingzhou Lunyu could have made free use of abbreviated variants of graphs that in standard forms of classical were normally written with disambiguating determinatives.7 Much of the fuzziness in the authors' discussion of the history of Chinese arises from their unqualified assertion that the language is an "analytic" one (p. 301). True enough, written and spoken Chinese now appear to lack inflection, and make meaningful sentences by controlling word order. But historical phonology, a discipline the authors never mention, has demonstrated the existence of a number of significant morphological features in spoken Old Chinese, certain of which certainly survived in the Warring States period, when the Lunyu was taking shape.8 A Lunyu aphorism read aloud in Mandarin may make little sense, at least for listeners whose education has not encouraged them to remember its sense; but the same aphorism read aloud in the Chinese of Confucius's day, or Mencius's, would have generated a good deal more phonetic information, and would rarely have been ambiguous, particularly given the specific contextual constraints that teaching and philosophical discussion no doubt imposed. If, as the authors believe, the credibility of their philosophical argument and their translation depends upon the success of the visual hypothesis (see again p. 285), then the failure of this hypothesis casts doubt on everything that follows from it. As I have noted, however, the hypothesis all but disappears in the course of the translation, and is not adduced in the interpretation of specific passages from the Lunyu. This is perhaps because, as a false conjecture, it is useless. Where the hypothesis does appear to affect the translation is in the authors' choices of equivalents for certain key terms; it should be noted again that this level, the lexical level, has nothing to tell us about putative visual principles of syntax. Like many of the translations under review, this one includes a discussion of key terms ("The Chinese Lexicon," pp. 45-65). Starting in most cases with an analysis of the graph used to represent the word, the authors discuss dao M 7See p. 231, n. 20; p. 235, n. 56; p. 265, n. 288. 8The subject is presented accessibly in Boltz, "Language and Writing," pp. 91-95. For a full treatment, see Laurent Sagart, The Roots of Old Chinese, Amsterdam Studies in the Theory and History of Linguistic Science, Vol. 184 (Amsterdam/Philadelphia: John Benjamins Publishing Company, 1999). SCHABERG Recent Translations of Lunyu 123 ("way" in their version), tian T, (romanized, not translated), ren I ("authoritative conduct"), li 1 ("observing ritual propriety"), yi A ("appropriate, fitting"), zhi V /t1 ("to realize, realization"), he fH ("harmony"), de {t ("excellence"), shan = ("truly adept, ability"), wen -( ("culture"), xiao j ("filial piety"), and several less central terms. The authors are to be applauded for offering clear justifications for their renditions of these key terms, and for using these consistently throughout their translation; some, like Lau, translate key terms inconsistently and thus make it practically impossible for non-Chinese-readers to consider the whole semantic range of a term. Yet, like most of the other translators, Ames and Rosemont confuse graphic analysis with etymology. Believing that classical Chinese was "like the good little boy: it was primarily to be seen and not heard" (p. 38), they reason from the components of graphs-not words, but conventional ways of writing words-while ignoring the real source of etymological evidence, which is found in word families. If the little boy was inclined to speak, they silence him by refusing to listen. There is a lost opportunity here, since a Lunyu translation that took scientific etymologies into account might well reveal many otherwise invisible relations among the words of the text. On the other hand, little new harm is done, since for the most part Ames and Rosemont do not allow interpretations derived from graphic analysis to supplant commonplace interpretations, which are more securely grounded in observations of uses and contexts. One or two of Ames's and Rosemont's choices are jarring. "Authoritative conduct," for instance, is at once too vague and, despite disclaimers (pp. 50-51), too suggestive of some benign and blinding tyranny.9 This choice of translation, along with that of several other terms, is most clearly motivated by the philosophical aims of the project, which require that the virtue most stressed in Lunyu Confucianism be made relevant to a transnational communitarian perspective inspired by John Dewey's pragmatism.10 This is not the right place to evaluate the promise of that project, but I will observe that Ames's and Rosemont's translation and all its terms are-necessarily, like any other translation-suspended somewhere between origins and uses. All translations of Lunyu are efforts to rewrite the text for new ends, and the question is not so much whether they are faithful, but whether they promised to be faithful, and in exactly what way, and whether they kept that particular promise. A communitarian Lunyu might be worth a lot, even if it required certain blatant infidelities or secretly broken promises of fidelity. One would only fault it to the extent that it lied about having support in Warring States realities. As it turns out, Ames's and Rosemont's translation itself is quite creditable, and holds its own even after the visual hypothesis is discounted. The Lunyu can do much 9"To realize" is also questionable, at least in its sense of "to make real," which Ames and Rosemont also intend. Zhi %1 does not, in the Lunyu, denote the transition of something from unreality to reality, but the new or continued awareness of something real that might have been unrecognized. 10This project is foregrounded in one of the several books Ames wrote with the late David L. Hall, The Democracy of the Dead: Dewey, Confucius, and the Hope for Democracy in China (Chicago: Open Court, 1999). All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

124 Chinese Literature: Essays, Articles, Reviews 23 (2001) of what they want it to do, and without egregious distortion of its original meanings. Consider the following passage from Lunyu 12.1: Yan Hui inquired about authoritative conduct (ren f?). The Master replied, "Through self-discipline and observing ritual propriety (ii ) one becomes authoritative in one's conduct. If for the space of a day one were able to accomplish this, the whole empire would defer to this authoritative model. Becoming authoritative in one's conduct is self-originating-how could it originate with others? This will not appeal to all tastes: it is wordy, and creates a jargony effect by turning verb-phrases into nouns and participles ("self-discipline," "self-originating"). It may lay too much emphasis on "becoming" authoritative, where wei ren A)AY_ quite possibly means (to use their term) "being authoritative" or "acting authoritatively."" But it is plausible, and will further speak directly to readers who have picked up the Lunyu for the sake of its promise as communitarian scripture. What strikes one reader as jargon impresses another as a dignified terminology capable of supporting new types of East-West philosophical exchange.12 And since Ames and Rosemont make their main innovations in their translations of individual terms, rather than in their handling of controversial passages, the accommodation of the Lunyu to this philosophy does not lead to many stunning departures from traditional interpretations. It only casts the latter in a new language.13 Ames and Rosemont set out to explain the truth about classical Chinese and its philosophical implications, then to translate the Lunyu in accordance with insights they have reached. It is a great irony that in positioning themselves against what they 11The strongest indication that in this case wei ren meant "being" rather than "becoming" ren is a near parallel to this passage found in Zuozhuan, Zhao 12. Ames and Rosemont do cite this passage (p. 249, n. 188), but they mistranslate it as if it were identical to the Lunyu passage. In fact it reads 'fi~~ i ,?: ""To overcome one's self and to restore ritual propriety: that is ren." It apparently has nothing to do with "becoming," and suggests at least the possibility that the same is true in Lunyu 12.1, where wei ren is ambiguous. 12In the continuation to the note mentioned above, Ames and Rosemont discuss the phrase ke ji j t: ".. . [T]he Zuo passage is rather clear evidence that it means 'self-discipline' in this instance. It is important not to 'naturalize' a notion of 'ego-self' that then has to be overcome. Rather, this is an inchoate, incipient, and radically embedded 'self' that needs cultivation and extension" (pp. 249-50, n. 188). The translation is competent, and qua translation even the jargon is acceptable. But to the extent that the authors claim, through their untenable visual hypothesis, to have captured timeless truths about Confucian thought, and to have rendered these faithfully in the terms they have chosen, they have profited improperly from an illusion of historical accuracy and authenticity. Most symptomatic of this procedure is the treatment of the Dingzhou texts. The cover copy states that the translation is based upon these and other archaeological finds, and, with the back cover blurb, strongly implies that consulting these texts has made possible a nearer approach to the "spirit and values" of the real Confucius. But in point of fact, the translation is based upon the received text, not upon the archaeological finds; and while Ames and Rosemont cite such finds in their notes to the translation, they very rarely find significant variations, and even more rarely follow them. Thus, despite the appeal to history that mention of the Dingzhou texts represents, this translation is more completely divorced from early Chinese intellectual and textual history than most of the others under review. One is forced to wonder if the promise of Confucianism as a twenty-first century philosophy somehow depends upon a strategic neglect of many known particulars of early Chinese writing and thought.14 Must Confucianism lose its history in order to serve ours? Tending the Classic Most of the translations under review are less ambitious than Ames's and Rosemont's, and seek not to change the course of intellectual history, but only to make the Lunyu available to new readers in new contexts. To repeat, the commercial viability of these efforts in no way undermines their usefulness: presumably, the increased pace of publication reflects an increased demand for knowledge of the Lunyu, and the distinctions that make each new translation unique correspond somehow to differing tastes among readers. These distinctions are made for the most part on the level of English style, not on the level of translation: with one exception, all of the translations in this group stick closely to received interpretations, differing occasionally in their choice of one over another, but rarely straying from paths laid out in the Lunyu's long commentarial tradition. As yet, no translation outdoes the commentaries through rigorous application of linguistic and epigraphic discoveries, and it is therefore natural that most contributions, including the most acceptable ones, are stylistically new variations on old themes. Stylistic differences are not necessarily minor differences. One suspects that the historical Confucius would have dispensed with the egalitarian pretensions. Huang Chichung's translation, like Raymond Dawson's, comes with a minimum of philosophical or reformist zeal. It claims only to be "literal," and largely succeeds in that aim, though not as consistently as Dawson does. What sets Huang's work apart from the others is his conscientiousness about citing alternative interpretations where these are viable. Much that is recorded in the Lunyu is quite obviously designed for a readership that already understands the import and context of a saying; large portions of the text might be described as esoteric, in the sense that they are designed for use in an educational setting that would have ruled out ambiguities. More consistently than any other translator, Huang uses his notes (helpfully placed, like those of Lau and of Brooks and Brooks, directly after each saying) to present evidence for his own interpretations and what he calls "'variant readings," i.e. other ways of construing the sayings. As noted above, traditional commentary has settled on a number of such alternate construals, particularly for the most lapidary sayings, and it is both simple and helpful to present them along with the interpretation of choice, in a sort of variorum translation. Where Huang's translation falls short is in its Introduction, which is full of historical simplifications and errors, and in its account of basic terminology, which exaggerates the coherence of a Confucian tradition encompassing Lunyu and much later texts. Like Ames and Rosemont, Huang understands "etymology" to mean graphic analysis, and he is comfortable citing late dictionaries like Cihai • for definitions of terms. His translations for these terms are mostly unsurprising, though "wholehearted sincerity" for zhong , (pp. 21-24) seems misleading, and in any case may usurp the place reserved for another important Confucian term, cheng M. Like Ames and Rosemont, though perhaps less openly, Brooks and Brooks stake the value of their work on a set of initial hypotheses, which, when they fail, threaten to bring down the whole edifice. First, a note on the contents of The Original Analects. Besides front matter (a brief preface and slightly longer introduction to Eastern Zhou history, schools, and texts) and translation of all passages of the received Lunyu, the work includes an introductory remark on each book and a fairly extensive comment on each passage. Following the translation are four Appendices: one on the Brookses' "accretion theory" as it applies to the Lunyu; one on the developmental patterns (e.g., the increasing wealth and power attributed to Confucius) that become apparent in the Lunyu when the books are put in what the authors take to be their original order of composition; one on connections between a historicized Lunyu and other texts of the so-called "Hundred Schools;" one on Confucius and his circle, which attempts to isolate historical facts about the man, his family, and his followers from amidst the welter of legend that has surrounded them; and, finally, a retranslation and commentary on Lunyu Books 1-4, showing how the received order differs in its philosophical implications from the "original" order. To be shown what Brooks and Brooks have promised to show, one must accept the following premises, all of them faulty: 1. One must accept that ancient Chinese texts grew like trees, and can be dated by a variety of textual dendrochronology. This version of the hypothesis thus implies that the beginnings of the Analects may indeed go back to a point of contact with the historical Confucius (a possibility doubted by several recent scholars), and that the typical leader of the school, whether later leaders succeeded by birth or were designated by their predecessors, contributed not one, but more than one, chapter module to the accumulating text. As a set of premises it may perhaps draw confirmation from other sorts of data, but as tautology it cannot be adduced in support of anything. An undefended assumption behind the tautology is that the Lunyu grew as a single corpus, with each generation taking over and adding to the material passed on by the previous generation. A moment's reflection reveals just how unlikely this is as an account of the early transmission of the Lunyu. Even if there had been only one prominent group of self-identified followers of Confucius's way during the Warring States period (and it is common knowledge that there were many more than one), the Brooks theory would still require either (1) that all extant Lunyu texts were updated each generation to reflect the most recent additions-clearly an impossibility-or (2) that this group's one master text came into the hands of Han Confucians to serve as the basis of our received text, and at that moment displaced any defective or variant versions that had lingered from former times. At first sight this second possibility has some promise, since our Lunyu must after all have come from somewhere. But the evidence does not cooperate. If a single, authoritative group of Confucians had been engaged, over nine generations, in the enlargement and refinement of Confucius's aphoristic works, then we may not expect them to have advertised the fact (as we will see, theories of authorial subterfuge and interpolation figure heavily in the Brooks interpretation); but we would at least expect them to have begun referring to this corpus by a single name. The earliest appearances of Lunyu as a book title, indicating the existence of a recognized corpus of authoritative material, come in the middle of the second century B.C., and early citations of Confucius's words (e.g. in the Mengzi K-T) show no particular fidelity to the materials now found in the Lunyu.26 On the basis of the available evidence, one might argue that the Lunyu was put together from multiple collections of Confucian aphorisms sometime in the early Han, and that during the Warring States no single collection held sway.27 The Brookses' assumption about a unitary corpus is barely acknowledged, perhaps because it must either be defended or abandoned if the strong form of the accretional hypothesis is to stand. 2. (p. 204) Again, to summarize: two separate kinds of data, one concerning the speakers to whom sayings are attributed, another concerning the linguistic nature of the sayings themselves, seem to support the same conclusion about the content of Lunyu 4. Quantification and statistical manipulation suggest differences between early and later portions of that chapter. Appearances are once again deceptive. The word si 1ff (to give it its pinyin romanization) may or may not be a sign of the age of a saying or its dialect associations. It is quite true that it does not occur in 4.18-25. But what of 4.26, which Brooks and Brooks have already dismissed as an interpolation? That saying, despite its attribution to Ziyou # - , uses si twice, and with precisely the same sense as in 4.7.29 Is 4.26 then more likely to be an early saying, or does the unsupported assertion that the core of Lunyu 4 contained only sayings of Confucius somehow trump the linguistic arguments? If si is an index of antiquity, then what are we to make of the use of this word, in the same sense, in 16.9, 20.2, and elsewhere in chapters generally agreed to be late? In what is unfortunately a sort of unofficial sinological tradition, Brooks and Brooks employ quasi-statistical methods and expressions even where they have gathered too little data to support any demonstrably significant results. Just as looking at the behavior of si outside of Lunyu 4.1-25 undermines the Brooks analysis of the chapter, counting predicates elsewhere in the text also calls into question the statistical treatment of this chapter. In a randomly chosen sample from a chapter thought to be very late-19.1-10-I find a total of 36 predicates, 23 of them (or 64%) nominal. From this I can draw no conclusion whatsoever about the relative antiquity of these passages: no one, least of all Brooks and Brooks, has taken the trouble to quantify all of the Lunyu's grammatical features, so it is impossible to say whether this figure belongs to a pattern, 294.7: y-• : •,•-_ t•' •r• , •1•' ,•I•. 4.26: '•F3 : •.• . ; 881• All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

Nonetheless, the figure 64% does put paid to the claim that the purported decrease from 81% to 40% in separate portions of Lunyu 4.1-25 is a consequence of the relative age of those portions. This is not to say that the grammatical shift Brooks and Brooks refer to did not occur, only that it is of little or no use when applied in ad hoc fashion to isolated portions of text, without comparative evidence from similar passages, and without consideration of the contents of the text. Symptoms, when they are useful in diagnosis, are useful because they can be related to a disease with known, predictable characteristics; behind the particular act of interpretation lies a science, nosology, that discourages wild guessing. Diagnosis without science, without even an attempt to gather the relevant data, would be quackery. 3. One must accept that every saying in the Lunyu was invented, transcribed, and incorporated into the work in the time it took to add one chapter, a period ranging from four years (for Chapter 20, here dated to 0249) to 31 years (for Chapter 9). In no case do Brooks and Brooks envision the incorporation in one chapter of a saying that was invented before the composition of the previous chapter. In other words, they all but completely rule out oral transmission, shifting the burden of generating new text from the total group of followers to the "head" of the unitary "school," whose views are supposed to be represented in the chapters dated to his tenure. Like some other assumptions, this one is neither acknowledged nor discussed, and in several respects defies logic. The structure of the school(s) is not nearly as well understood as Brooks and Brooks imply, and if there ever was a single paramount leader, it is by no means certain that he exercised the authority to alter the putative proto-Lunyu at will, much less to suppress whatever knowledge of the past other followers were transmitting and inventing. To suggest that every saying is datable, and to a window of at most 31 years, is to ignore much relevant comparative evidence, which suggests that attempts to codify the teaching of a revered sage draw selectively from complex traditions of lore relating to that sage, and that no single act of transcription stops the transmission and variation of the lore. If lore can survive beyond the succession of a new school leader, then the very attempt to date Lunyu chapters precisely according to their contents is doomed. Since much of the point of The Original Analects is to identify "interpolations" (usually on the basis of the faintest hint of external historical evidence, or on the basis of the faulty assumptions already examined), the notion that one generation might write down a saying learned from a previous generation is fatal to the whole project. 4. One must accept a novel view of the internal structuring of Lunyu chapters. Brooks and Brooks argue the following: Earlier commentators have noted close relations between specific pairs of Analects sayings, though it has not been appreciated that such pairing, admittedly often based on trivial features, characterizes the entire text, giving it a background against which disruptive interpolated sayings can be relatively easily recognized. SCHABERG Recent Translations of Lunyu 137 pairing based on "trivial features" is a feature not of the Lunyu, but of The Original Analects." If, as the strong form of the accretional hypothesis requires, sayings originated and were transcribed in the span of years separating successive chapters, what wealth of material did school-heads draw on as they constructed their pairs? If they had the liberty to make up material (as Brooks and Brooks sometimes seem to believe), then why did they not more frequently make less trivial pairings? Rather than postulating the silent continuation of a compositional practice over nine generations and 19 very diverse books, why not remark it where it is undeniable and leave it in question where it seems contrived? The only apparent justification for the totalizing assertion about pairing is the spurious support it gives to charges that one or another passage is an "interpolation"; since historical and linguistic data for these charges are minimal or nil, the pairing hypothesis is adduced as an independent source of information. But because the criteria adduced for identifying a pair are extremely loose and apparently made ad hoc (as they must be if the hypothesis is to be defended throughout the Lunyu), the hypothesis is ultimately unfalsifiable: the paragraphs of my review are every bit as "paired" as the aphorisms of the Brooks and Brooks Lunyu. 5. One must accept tendentious, largely unsupported datings of other early Chinese texts. In a two-page "checklist of texts," Brooks and Brooks do not bother to cite alternative views, or often even to hint at the complexities of dating issues: DJ (Dzwo Jwan) [i.e. Zuozhuan]. A supplement to the CC [Chunqiu fI], begun in Lu in c0350; the present text is a Chi-adapted expansion of c0312. Gives a retrospective picture of Spring and Autumn life, apparently blended with details from the late 04c. Justly esteemed as a narrative, but must be used cautiously as a source. Translated in Legge Ch'un. (p. 8) Shr (The [Classic of] Poetry) [i.e. Shijing]. Compiled (and, we argue, mostly written) from the middle 05c to the late 04c; one can watch from the evolving Analects as it reaches its final 305-poem size. Translated in Legge She and Waley Songs. (p. 9) Brooks and Brooks cite no defense for these surprising claims. The untutored and the credulous will assume either that the relevant dating questions were solved long ago, or that Brooks and Brooks have solved them themselves. The critical will hesitate to credit the assertions, given the quality of historical arguments advanced elsewhere in the work. More trivially, one must believe that pinyin is inaccessible enough to the ordinary reader to justify the invention of a new, putatively more accessible system, the Common Alphabet: Chinese words are here spelled for maximum "guessability" by readers with English- alphabet reflexes. The rule is "consonants as in English, vowels as in Italian," with a few special conventions, such as v (an analogue of the linguist's inverted v) for the central vowel of "gut," plus ae as in "cat," r as in "fur," z as in "adz," and yw (after 1 or n, simply w) for "umlaut u." (p. 2) This system might possibly be an improvement over pinyin if all of us, generalists included, were starting from zero. But anyone who has, say, watched network news or listened to the radio a few times during the past years already knows how to approximate the pinyin "e" and "x" (as in "Deng Xiaoping"), "j" and "z" (as in "Jiang Zemin"); he or she can also distinguish two types of -ia- ("Tiananmen" versus "Jiang"), and may plausibly slur through "Zhou Enlai." If people have not drunk enough imported beer to know how "q" might work, it is only a matter of time before a high-profile leader or crisis makes this and the rest of pinyin easier for most educated Americans to deal with than French. Since pinyin is for practical purposes already pretty well-known, the Common Alphabet defeats its own purpose. It will not "help to dispel the 'Oriental mystique' which several aggressively nonphonetic Chinese spelling systems have helped to promote" (p. 2), but will instead begin to restore a mystique that pinyin is on the verge of losing. Pronouncements about the Common Alphabet do, with other elements (such as the checklist of texts, the unique dating and citation conventions, and the special signs used to represent pairings and interpolations of sayings), lend a scientific feel to the project, as if a new rigor were being introduced into a disorderly old field. But for most readers, the romanization conventions will serve only as a distraction and an annoyance, and will tend to divert attention from truly scientific questions of philological method. This list could perhaps be extended. The Original Analects is so bold, so original, and so conjectural that it demands a sort of surrender, even from readers who have not already invested in the disciplinary commonplaces of sinology. To my mind, however, any one of the listed concessions requires too great a sacrifice of methodological rigor on the reader's part, and the whole performance costs much more than it is worth. The translation itself-once one gets used to the Common Alphabet-is both accurate and readable, and benefits from the same clarity and vigor that characterize the Brookses' English elsewhere in the book. Although the comments Brooks and Brooks append to each saying are too frequently dominated by specious arguments for pairing of sayings or by irrelevancies (like citations from British texts on aristocratic life, supposed to illuminate Warring States attitudes by comparison), they are admirable in being designed to "slow the general reader down" (p. viii), and often contain useful insights. Finally, however, The Original Analects lives and dies by its claim to give us the sayings of Warring States followers of Confucius in their original historical order. SCHABERG Recent Translations of Lunyu 139 Read against itself-as a hoax, for instance, if that were possible-the book would deliver a stinging reproof to practitioners of many of the laziest techniques of provenance studies. But as a serious effort to historicize the Lunyu, the book does not support its own arguments, much less the larger project of dating all Warring States texts. To conclude, if this survey of the Lunyu translations currently on offer seems almost unrelievedly negative, that is because what this important text deserves it has not yet gotten: a translation that combines linguistic, philological, and historical competence in equal measure, that appeals without pandering, and that does justice to the work's intellectual force without seeking to denature or dilute it. The several strengths of the translations under review, and the fact that so many translations could have been published in so short a time, are an encouragement, and will no doubt do much to advance the reputation of the Lunyu among English-speaking readers. But as we look forward to some translation that will outdo them all, let us not be deceived. If someone offers to sell you the real Confucius, the original, the literal, the acceptable, the reformist, even the historically and linguistically competent, be suspicious: the article itself, the true jade, is lost, and the honest merchant will tell you so.
